Amongst the Deputies of the Chambers, our readers, perhaps, have remarked that there are few remarkable tor splendid talents or genius. There are no men of the same calibre as the leading members of the National Assembly, tbe constituent Assembly, or the Convention þÿ and this, instead of being subject a of lamentation or regret, is, with us, a subject of congratulation and hope. The French want rone of those brilliant but wild imaginations which despise the path of common sense, aspire to the boldest flights, soar into the regions of speculation and theory, fancy themselves to have found out the up some fine system philosopher's stone in in politics, which man is to and build arrive at perfection, to reach the utmost point of perfectability, Of the vanity of all these theories; of the excesses to which they must always lead, surely the Fiench must be convinced at las. They want men, not of brilliant, but of solid parts þÿ men of prudence and moderation þÿ men who are not anxious to he at the head of parties þÿ to make the Legislative Assembly the scene of struggles for power and ambition ; but, who, seeing and feeling the deep wounds of their country, are desirous only of finding out and applying the most effectual remedy. We had a Parliament in England to which was applied the epithet of healing. þÿ It was the healing Parliament. May history have to apply this blessed epithet to the Legislature of France ! In explaining closely the present con-

jecture, perhaps we shall find it by no means unfavourable to tbe adoption of wise and prudent measures. Tiie party which was most to he dreaded, has, in a great measure lost, if not its principles, at least its hopes þÿ aud can no longer look for support to that army which it was once feared might involve France in (he double horrors of foreign and civil war. The reiv Ministers are men who do not recal any terrible recollections to the mind men who are worthy to serve as the middle point between a King who wishes to bury everv thing in oblivion, and the representatives of a people who feel all the duties which such a conduct on the part of the King enjoiiss upon them. It had become necessary that the Ministers of the King should choose at an epoch in which the peace of Europe is about to be ensured by a definitive treaty, should afford to the Allied Powers by tii« purity of tbeir principles, a sufficient guarantee for the duration of a repose which lias been at length established with such difficulty. The King has- formed a Ministry which Combines all these advantages, which is presided by a man whose name is connected with the history of the Monarchy, and tt&o, honored with the confidence of ano-

ther grrat orereign, ceased for a tune to be a Frenchman, only that he might be better able to serve Fiance, regenerated, and delivered. Another great advantage is, i hat the new Ministry is so composed, as to render any idea ot a re-action, which is ns contrury to the sentiments of the King aud his family, as it is to the sentiments of the whole nation, impracticable. The Prime Minister is personally a stranger to all the troubles that have desolated F ranee ; aud Ins colleagues, known tor their moderation aud integrity, so tar from having anv vengeance to execute, can only feel gratitude for bejng placed in situations in w hich they are permitted to render such service to their Cnuntry. Less of course can be said with certainty of the opinions and principles of these Deputies, but as they are know n to have played no marked or prominent parts in the Revolution, we may safely infer that they must be anxious to heal the wounds it lias produced. Seeing this, the King, the Legislature, and the Ministers, united by one principle, it may be permitted us to hope, that the measures which wiil result from the Session of the tw-o Chambers, will produce the double effect of confirming the repose of France, and of giving confidence to the Allies, One of the late military meetings of the Allied Sovereigns was terminated by a kind of religious cerimony, in which they pledged themselves to labor for (fie happiness of the people entrusted to their Governments, and to mantain the peace

of the world. May that heaVen w hich recognised their oath; never have their breach to punish. The witnesses of this solemn and touching scene agree in stating, that the chivalrous graces of Alexander, and his noble enthusiasm tor grand and generous ideas, gave it a particular charm. <::>- York Of the Canadas. þÿ Gazette, who signs, A writer in the New-- þÿ A Traveller þÿ, has commented on the remarks made in þÿ the Ceutiuel on his reports from th Canadas. The only part of the new text of the þÿ þÿTraveller, w hich requires notice, þÿ is the repetition of his intimation, þÿ That the British military officers in Canada, expected that the now Governor-General, Murray, would bring out with him a reinforcement of 10,000 troops, Svc. And we repeat, on the information of gentlemen of intelligence and veracity from Canada, that no such reinforcement was expected there; and that none had recently arrived but recruits from the depots at home. We think it additional evidence of the truth of our information, that troops from Canada were continually arriving in England ; not to say any thing of the improbability that the British Ministry would incur the heavy expense of their double transportation. We have before us two late English papers, in which are accounts of the arrival in October, of transports from Quebec full of

troops; and as late as the ISih of that month, the ship Traave was spoken, als» full of them. We can also repeat, that all late appearances in Canada, wore th aspect of an expected long continuance of peace. Truth is our object; þÿ audit is as much a duty to guard against undue alarm as uudue security.

Arch -Bishop Carrot, t, was torn at Upper Marlborough, in the State of Maryland, in the year 1735, and was sent at the age of ten or twelve years, to a grammar school at Bohemia, in Cecil county. Even at this early period, lie gave strik- 'tg presages of his future worth and eminence, by the mildness and innocence of his manners, his docility and assiduity. I le also kept a journal of his travels, which strikingly displays that

good sense, sound judgment, and enlightened intelligence, which ever distinguished him. Upon his return to England, he resided for some time in the family of Lord Nobleman) when upon the approach of the revolutionary war, he withstood the earnest and pressing solicitations of his noble and benificent patron, and came back to his native country. Shortly after his return, at the request of (lie American Congress, he accom- Sunday last, i Carrollton (his relative and friend) panied Dr. Franklin, Charles Carroll of and the late Judge Chase, on a political mission to Canada. And throughout the arduous and hazardous conflict which ensued he remained fervently attached to the cause of ll is country. He did not at anytime, however, neglect his clerical duties, the primary object of his care and solicitude. Upon his arrival in bis native country, he lost no tune in taking upon himself the laborious caie of several Catholic congregations widely separated from eatli other; where his memory is cherished with the most enthusiastic affection.
